[Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace") is the official residence of the president of the Philippines, a privilege entitled to him/her under Article VII, Section 6 of the Constitution.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Const-7) The palace is located along the north bank of the [Pasig River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasig_River "Pasig River"), along J.P. Laurel Street in the district of [San Miguel, Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Miguel,_Manila "San Miguel, Manila"). The [Filipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_language "Filipino language") name is derived from the [Tagalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagalog_language "Tagalog language") phrase "_may [lakán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakan "Lakan") diyán_" ("there is a [nobleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobility#Filipino "Nobility") there"), and this was eventually shortened to _Malakanyáng_. The complex includes several mansions and office buildings built and designed in the _[bahay na bato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahay\_na\_bato "Bahay na bato")_ and [neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-classical_architecture "Neo-classical architecture") architectural styles.

Before Malacañang Palace was designated as the official residence of the president, various establishments served as residence of the chief executive in the Philippines. The Spanish governor-general, the highest-ranking official in the Philippines during the Spanish Era, resided in the [Palacio del Gobernador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palacio_del_Gobernador "Palacio del Gobernador") inside the walled city of [Intramuros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intramuros "Intramuros"). However, after an [earthquake in 1863](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1863_Manila_earthquake "1863 Manila earthquake"), the Palacio del Gobernador was destroyed, and the residence and office of the governor-general was transferred to Malacañang Palace. During the [Philippine Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Revolution "Philippine Revolution"), Aguinaldo resided in various places in [Cavite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavite "Cavite") before establishing [Malolos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malolos "Malolos"), Bulacan as capital, and he would be inaugurated as President of the First Republic here. During the [Philippine-American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine-American_War "Philippine-American War"), Aguinaldo successively established [new capitals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_of_the_Philippines "Capital of the Philippines") as he retreated northward in the face of invading American forces.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-131) When the Americans occupied the Philippines, they also used Malacañang Palace as an official residence for their governors-general. During the [Japanese occupation of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_occupation_of_the_Philippines "Japanese occupation of the Philippines"), the presidential seat and government offices were transferred to the more inland Baguio, where the [Mansion House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mansion,_Baguio "The Mansion, Baguio") was used as the official residence. Meanwhile, President [Manuel L. Quezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_L._Quezon "Manuel L. Quezon") of the [Philippine Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_the_Philippines "Commonwealth of the Philippines")[government-in-exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government-in-exile "Government-in-exile") resided in the [Omni Shoreham Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omni_Shoreham_Hotel "Omni Shoreham Hotel") in [Washington D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_D.C. "Washington D.C.") After the restoration of independence in 1946, plans were made for the construction of the new presidential residence to replace Malacañang in [a new capital city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_City "Quezon City"). However, the plans did not push through and the president's official residence is still Malacañang Palace in Manila.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-132)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-133)

A secondary residence within the wider palace grounds is _[Bahay Pangulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahay\_Pangulo "Bahay Pangulo")_ (transl.President's House), formerly known as _Bahay Pangarap_ (transl.House of Dreams) and _Bahay ng Pagbabago_ (transl.House of Change),[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Bahay_Pangarap:_Aquino's_future_home?-134) a smaller structure located on the south bank of the [Pasig River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasig_River "Pasig River") across the main palace in [Malacañang Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Park "Malacañang Park"),[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-How_was_PNoy's_first_night_at_Bahay_Pangarap?-135) which is itself part of the [Presidential Security Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Security_Group "Presidential Security Group") Complex.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Bahay_Pangarap:_Aquino's_future_home?-134)[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Noynoy's_new_home_is_Bahay_Pangarap-136) President [Benigno Aquino III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_III "Benigno Aquino III") was the first to use _Bahay Pangarap_ as his official residence.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Bahay_Pangarap_for_P-Noy_ready-137)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Briefer_on_Bahay_Pangarap_and_Malaca%C3%B1ang_Park-138) It was originally built in the 1930s under President Quezon as a rest house and venue for informal activities and social functions of the First Family.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Bahay_Pangarap:_Aquino's_future_home?-134)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Briefer_on_Bahay_Pangarap_and_Malaca%C3%B1ang_Park-138) The house was designed by architect Juan Arellano in the 1930s,[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Bahay_Pangarap:_Aquino's_future_home?-134)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Briefer_on_Bahay_Pangarap_and_Malaca%C3%B1ang_Park-138) and underwent several renovations in the early 1960s, 2008, and 2010.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Bahay_Pangarap:_Aquino's_future_home?-134)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-How_was_PNoy's_first_night_at_Bahay_Pangarap?-135)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Briefer_on_Bahay_Pangarap_and_Malaca%C3%B1ang_Park-138)

The president also has several other official residences nationwide for official use. [The Mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mansion_(Baguio) "The Mansion (Baguio)") in [Baguio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baguio "Baguio") is the official [summer palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Palace "Summer Palace") of the president. The palace was originally built in 1908 to serve as the summer residence for American [Governors-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_the_Philippines "Governor-General of the Philippines"), and later became the holiday home and working office for presidents when the government would temporarily visit Baguio.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-marker-139)[Malacañang of the South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_of_the_South "Malacañang of the South") in [Davao City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davao_City "Davao City") is the president's residence in [Mindanao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindanao "Mindanao"). It was built in 2005 on state property and serves as an official residence and base of operations for presidents when visiting Davao and the surrounding provinces. [Malacañang sa Sugbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_sa_Sugbo "Malacañang sa Sugbo") in [Cebu City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cebu_City "Cebu City") was the former official residence in [the Visayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visayas "Visayas"). Originally the local office of the [Bureau of Customs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Customs "Bureau of Customs") (BOC), it was converted to a palace in 2004. It was later returned to the BOC.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-140)[Malacañang of the North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_of_the_North "Malacañang of the North") was also an official residence of the president in the [Ilocos Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Region "Ilocos Region"). The residence is currently a presidential museum.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-PDI-141)

Whenever the President visits the [Clark Freeport Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Freeport_Zone "Clark Freeport Zone"), they stay at the White House, which was formerly the official residence of the Commanding General of the [13th Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteenth_Expeditionary_Air_Force "Thirteenth Expeditionary Air Force") during the time Clark was a [U.S. Air Force base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Air_Base "Clark Air Base").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Visit_Clark_-_White_House-142)[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Guide_to_the_PH_-_White_House-143) President [Manuel Roxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Roxas "Manuel Roxas") after reviewing troops on April 15, 1948, rested in the White House, but would later suffer a heart attack. Roxas death anniversary is commemorated annually at the White House.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Philstar:_Roxas-144)

### Travel

#### Air transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Air transportation")]

Main article: [Air transports of heads of state and government §Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_transports_of_heads_of_state_and_government#Philippines "Air transports of heads of state and government")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/PAF-Puma-at-Subic-Bay.JPEG/250px-PAF-Puma-at-Subic-Bay.JPEG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PAF-Puma-at-Subic-Bay.JPEG)

An [Aérospatiale SA-330 Puma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westland_Puma "Westland Puma") carrying President [Corazon C. Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino "Corazon Aquino") at [Subic Bay Naval Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subic_Bay_Naval_Base "Subic Bay Naval Base").

The 250th (Presidential) Airlift Wing of the [Philippine Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Air_Force "Philippine Air Force") has the mandate of providing safe and efficient air transport for the president of the Philippines and the First Family. On occasion, the wing has also been tasked to provide transportation for other members of government, visiting heads of state, and other state guests.

The majority of the fleet is fairly dated with a few exceptions it includes: 1 [Fokker F28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fokker_F28 "Fokker F28"), which is primarily used for the president's domestic trips and it is also called "Kalayaan One" when the president is on board, 4 [Bell 412](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_412 "Bell 412") helicopters, 3 [Sikorsky S-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikorsky_S-76 "Sikorsky S-76") helicopters, 1 [Sikorsky S-70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikorsky_S-70 "Sikorsky S-70")-5 Black Hawk, a number of [Bell UH-1N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_UH-1N "Bell UH-1N") Twin Hueys, as well as [Fokker F-27](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fokker_F-27 "Fokker F-27")_Friendship_ s. In September 2020, a new [Gulfstream G280](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulfstream_G280 "Gulfstream G280") was delivered which will be used for VIP transport as well as for C2 (Command and Control) missions.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-145) For trips outside of the Philippines, the Air Force employs a [Bombardier Global Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_Global_Express "Bombardier Global Express"), [Gulftsream G650ER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulftsream_G650ER?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gulftsream G650ER (page does not exist)") or charters appropriate aircraft from the country's flag carrier, [Philippine Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Airlines "Philippine Airlines"). Any PAL aircraft with the flight number "PR/PAL 001" and callsign "PHILIPPINE 001" is a flight operated by [Philippine Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Airlines "Philippine Airlines") to transport the president of the Philippines. The president sometimes charter private jets for domestic trips within the Philippines due to some airports in the Philippines having small runways.

**Vice President of the Philippines** ([Filipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_language "Filipino language"): _Pangalawang Pangulo ng Pilipinas_, also referred to as _Bise Presidente ng Pilipinas_) is the title of the second-highest official in the executive branch of the [Philippine government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_government "Philippine government") and is first in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_presidential_line_of_succession "Philippine presidential line of succession"). The vice president is [directly elected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_election "Direct election") by the [citizens of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipinos "Filipinos") and is one of only two nationally elected executive officials, the other being the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines").

The current office of the vice president was re-established under the [1987 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Philippines "Constitution of the Philippines"), bearing similarities with the office as created in the [1935 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_Constitution_of_the_Philippines "1935 Constitution of the Philippines") that was abolished by the [Marcos regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcos_regime "Marcos regime"). The vice president may be elected to two consecutive six-year terms. The 15th and incumbent vice president [Sara Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Duterte "Sara Duterte") was inaugurated on June 19, 2022,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-2) but her term officially began 11 days later on June 30, as per the constitution.

## Title

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Title")]

The official title of the office in Filipino is _Pangalawang Pangulo,_ although _Bise Presidente,_ derived from [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"), is the usual title used in some of the major [Philippine languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_the_Philippines "Languages of the Philippines"), such as [Cebuano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cebuano_language "Cebuano language") and [Hiligaynon language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiligaynon_language "Hiligaynon language"). The text of the 1987 Constitution refers to the person and office of the _vice-president,_ with a hyphen connecting the two words. However, the person and office is usually referred to today without the hyphen, as the _vice president_.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

### Colonial era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Colonial era")]

The first known vice president claiming to be part of a government was [Mariano Trías](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariano_Tr%C3%ADas "Mariano Trías"), whose term started on March 22, 1897. He was elected during the elections of the [Tejeros Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tejeros_Convention "Tejeros Convention"), and was later elected vice president of the Supreme Council that oversaw negotiations for the [Pact of Biak-na-Bato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pact_of_Biak-na-Bato "Pact of Biak-na-Bato") in 1897. This Supreme Council had no sovereignty, did not govern any state, and was just used for bargaining with the Spanish. This council was replaced later, with no such position existing during the country's declaration of independence in 1898, which had a dictatorial government. Officially, the country's first actual republic was founded in 1899, and it too had no vice president. Trias instead served in the cabinets of [Apolinario Mabini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apolinario_Mabini "Apolinario Mabini") and [Pedro Paterno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Paterno "Pedro Paterno"), as finance minister and war minister, respectively. Trias is not considered a Philippine vice president as the Supreme Council did not proclaim any sovereign state.

### Conceptualization and the Commonwealth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Conceptualization and the Commonwealth")]

The 1935 Constitution, largely patterned after the U.S. Constitution,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-3) provided the basis for the Commonwealth government. It also established the position of vice president, and as per Section 12, Subsection 3, the vice president may be appointed by the president to a cabinet position. But unlike their U.S. counterpart, the vice president is not the president of the Philippine senate as senators choose their president from among their ranks. The first person elected to the position of vice president under the constitution was [Sergio Osmeña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Osme%C3%B1a "Sergio Osmeña"), elected together with [Manuel L. Quezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_L._Quezon "Manuel L. Quezon") in the first Philippine national elections.

### Third Republic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Third Republic")]

Since the inception of the 1935 constitution, the president and vice president came from the same ticket and political party, until the [1957 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957_Philippine_presidential_election "1957 Philippine presidential election"), which saw the first-ever split ticket that won the presidency and vice presidency.

### Fourth Republic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Fourth Republic")]

The 1973 Constitution abolished the office of the vice president and [Fernando Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Lopez "Fernando Lopez") was therefore unable to finish his term. Subsequent amendments, particularly the [1984 amendments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Philippine_constitutional_plebiscite "1984 Philippine constitutional plebiscite") restored the vice presidency. [Arturo Tolentino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Tolentino "Arturo Tolentino") was officially proclaimed vice president-elect by the [Regular Batasang Pambansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_Batasang_Pambansa "Regular Batasang Pambansa") in 1986. He took his oath as vice president on February 16, 1986, before Chief Justice [Ramon Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Aquino "Ramon Aquino"), but because of popular belief that the elections had been rigged, he never actually served out his term as vice president. Within a week after Tolentino's oath, the [People Power Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_Power_Revolution "People Power Revolution") resulted in the collapse of the Marcos regime.

### Fifth Republic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Fifth Republic")]

The [People Power Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_Power_Revolution "People Power Revolution") installed [Corazon Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino "Corazon Aquino") into the presidency. On February 25, 1986, Aquino and her running mate, [Salvador Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Laurel "Salvador Laurel"), were sworn in as president and vice-president, respectively.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-4) Since the promulgation of the [1987 constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Philippines "Constitution of the Philippines"), only two elections have produced a president and a vice president from the same ticket: [Gloria Macapagal Arroyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Macapagal_Arroyo "Gloria Macapagal Arroyo") and [Noli de Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noli_de_Castro "Noli de Castro") in [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Philippine_presidential_election "2004 Philippine presidential election") and [Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos") and [Sara Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Duterte "Sara Duterte") in [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Philippine_presidential_election "2022 Philippine presidential election").

## Powers and roles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Powers and roles")]

Aside from being mandated to assume the presidency in case of the death, disability, or resignation of the incumbent president, the 1987 Constitution did not lay out any explicit powers for the vice president, giving rise to the office being called a "spare tire".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-5) Article 7, Section 3 of the Constitution provided, however, that the vice president may be appointed to a cabinet position, without the need for confirmation. Appointments usually must be confirmed by the [Commission on Appointments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commission_on_Appointments "Commission on Appointments"), as per Article 7, Section 16 of the Constitution.

### Cabinet member

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Cabinet member")]

Since the inception of the 1935 Constitution, vice presidents have been appointed to Cabinet positions, with a few rejecting the offer made by the seating president. Osmeña was given the highest-ranking cabinet portfolio with inauguration of the Commonwealth of the Philippines in November 1935. Prior to independence in 1946, that cabinet portfolio was Secretary of Public Instruction, which had once been reserved only for the vice governor-general (an American). Vice President Osmeña held that position from 1935 to 1939, and a similar portfolio in the War Cabinet during World War II.

| **14** | [Leni Robredo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leni_Robredo "Leni Robredo") | July 7, 2016 | December 5, 2016[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-13) | [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte") |

After independence, the highest-ranking cabinet position became that of secretary of foreign affairs (it is still the highest-ranking cabinet portfolio in official protocol to this day), which was given to Vice President [Elpidio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino "Elpidio Quirino"). Vice President [Fernando Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Lopez "Fernando Lopez") declined the foreign affairs portfolio when he became Quirino's vice president in 1949 and instead served as secretary of agriculture and natural resources during his two non-consecutive terms. However, Vice Presidents [Carlos P. Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_P._Garcia "Carlos P. Garcia") and [Emmanuel Pelaez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Pelaez "Emmanuel Pelaez") also held the foreign affairs portfolio, a tradition revived in the Fifth Republic, as well as Vice Presidents [Salvador Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Laurel "Salvador Laurel") and [Teofisto Guingona Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teofisto_Guingona_Jr. "Teofisto Guingona Jr.") after the position's restoration in 1986. [Gloria Macapagal Arroyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Macapagal_Arroyo "Gloria Macapagal Arroyo") served as secretary of social welfare and development and incumbent [Sara Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Duterte "Sara Duterte") served as the secretary of education. Other Cabinet positions with no secretary title was given to Vice President [Joseph Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Estrada "Joseph Estrada") as chairman of the Presidential Anti-Crime Commission and to Vice Presidents [Noli de Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noli_de_Castro "Noli de Castro"), [Jejomar Binay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jejomar_Binay "Jejomar Binay"), and [Leni Robredo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leni_Robredo "Leni Robredo") as chairman of the Housing and Urban Development Coordinating Council.

Among the vice presidents, [Diosdado Macapagal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diosdado_Macapagal "Diosdado Macapagal") alone was not given any cabinet position, since he was the first elected vice president that did not originate from the same party as the incumbent president.

### Successor to the Philippine president

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Successor to the Philippine president")]

The vice president is first in the presidential line of succession. The Constitution provides several circumstances where the vice president (or the vice president-elect) shall assume the presidency or serve as acting president.

*   In case of the death, permanent disability, removal from office, or resignation of the president, the vice president shall assume the presidency.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-14)
*   If the president-elect fails to qualify for office, the vice president-elect shall act as president until the president-elect is qualified.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Article_VII-15)
*   If in case of death, permanent disability, dismissed from service, resignation or failure to assume the post, the Senate president shall assume the vice presidency.
*   If a president is not chosen, then the vice president shall act as president until a president is chosen and qualified.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Article_VII-15)

There have been four cases where the vice president has assumed the presidency, three of which because of the president's death, and one because of the president's resignation:

*   [Sergio Osmeña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Osme%C3%B1a "Sergio Osmeña") in 1944, upon the death of [Manuel L. Quezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_L._Quezon "Manuel L. Quezon").
*   [Elpidio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino "Elpidio Quirino") in 1948, upon the death of [Manuel Roxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Roxas "Manuel Roxas").
*   [Carlos P. Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_P._Garcia "Carlos P. Garcia") in 1957, upon the death of [Ramon Magsaysay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay "Ramon Magsaysay").
*   [Gloria Macapagal Arroyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Macapagal_Arroyo "Gloria Macapagal Arroyo") in 2001, upon the resignation of [Joseph Ejercito Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Estrada "Joseph Estrada"), as decided by the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Supreme Court of the Philippines"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-16) following the events of the [Second EDSA Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_EDSA_Revolution "Second EDSA Revolution").

### Other roles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Other roles")]

Aside from their constitutional roles, the vice president may initiate various programs and services under the [Office of the Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Vice_President_of_the_Philippines "Office of the Vice President of the Philippines"). The vice president also performs ceremonial functions, occasionally representing the president, the government, and the country in official gatherings and diplomatic functions. The vice president was also a member of the [National Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Council_(Philippines) "National Security Council (Philippines)"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-EO34-17) until its reorganization in 2025 which removed the vice president from the body.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-18)

## Election process

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Election process")]

### Eligibility

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Eligibility")]

Article 7, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution mandates that the vice president must bear the same qualifications as the president which is:

*   a natural-born citizen of the Philippines
*   a registered voter
*   be able to read and write
*   at least forty years of age on the day of the election
*   a resident of the Philippines for at least ten years immediately preceding such election

Natural-born Filipinos are citizens of the Philippines from birth without having to perform any act to acquire or perfect their Philippine citizenship. Those whose fathers or mothers are citizens of the Philippines at the time of their birth and those born before January 17, 1973, of Filipino mothers, who elect Philippine citizenship upon reaching the age of majority are considered natural-born Filipinos.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-19)

### Election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Election")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Home_provinces_of_Philippine_vice_presidents_2022.jpg/250px-Home_provinces_of_Philippine_vice_presidents_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Home_provinces_of_Philippine_vice_presidents_2022.jpg)

Home provinces of the vice presidents

The vice president is elected in the same manner as, but separately from, the president: by direct vote every six years, usually on the second Monday of May.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-20) The latest election was held in [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Philippine_presidential_election "2022 Philippine presidential election").

Both the president and the vice president are elected by direct plurality vote where the candidate who garners the highest number of votes, whether a majority or not, wins the election.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-:1-21) While candidates usually run in tandem for the offices of president and vice president, under their own political parties, it is possible and not unusual for candidates from different parties to be elected as president and vice president; since the establishment of the Fifth Republic in 1986, only the elections of 2004 and 2022 had the winners come from a single ticket.

The returns of every election for president and vice president, duly certified by the board of canvassers of each province or city, shall be transmitted to Congress, directed to the president of the Senate. Upon receipt of the certificates of canvass, the president of the Senate shall open all the certificates in the presence of a joint public session of Congress not later than 30 days after election day. Congress then canvasses the votes upon determining that the polls are authentic and were done in the manner provided by law.

### Inauguration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Inauguration")]

Traditionally, the vice president takes the oath first, a little before noon for two reasons. First, according to protocol, no one follows the president (who is last due to his supremacy), and second, to establish a constitutionally valid successor before the president-elect accedes. During the [Quezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_L._Quezon "Manuel L. Quezon") inauguration, however, the vice president and legislature were sworn in after the president, to symbolize a new start. In 2016[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-22) and 2022,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-23) the inaugurations for president and vice president were held separately. Vice President-elect [Sara Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Duterte "Sara Duterte") broke tradition by taking oath on June 19, 2022, or days ahead prior to her scheduled assumption of office on June 30.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-24)

The vice president-elect recites an oath, similar to the one recited by the president-elect, as provided by the 1987 Constitution:

> "I, (name), do solemnly swear (or affirm), that I will faithfully and conscientiously fulfill my duties as President (or Vice President or Acting President) of the Philippines. Preserve and defend its Constitution, execute its laws, do justice to every man, and consecrate myself to the service of the Nation. So help me God." (In case of affirmation, last sentence will be omitted.) — Constitution of the Philippines, art. 7, sec. 5

The Filipino text of the oath used for the inaugurations of presidents [Fidel V. Ramos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_V._Ramos "Fidel V. Ramos"), [Joseph Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Estrada "Joseph Estrada"), [Benigno Aquino III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_III "Benigno Aquino III"), and [Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos") reads:

> "Ako si (pangalan), ay taimtim kong pinanunumpaan (o pinatototohanan) na tutuparin ko nang buong katapatan at sigasig ang aking mga tungkulin bilang Pangulo (o Pangalawang Pangulo o Nanunungkulang Pangulo) ng Pilipinas, pangangalagaan at ipagtatanggol ang kanyang Konstitusyon, ipatutupad ang mga batas nito, magiging makatarungan sa bawat tao, at itatalaga ang aking sarili sa paglilingkod sa Bansa. Kasihan nawa ako ng Diyos." (Kapag pagpapatotoo, ang huling pangungusap ay kakaltasin. — Konstitusyon ng Pilipinas, Artikulo VII, SEK. 5

Traditionally, the language that the incoming president uses for his oath shall also be the one used by the incoming vice president.

## Incumbency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Incumbency")]

### Term limits

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Term limits")]

Under the 1935 Constitutions, the vice president, along with the president, set the vice president's term at six years, with possibility of re-election as only the president was barred from seeking re-election.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-25) In 1940, it shortened the term from six to four years, again without limitations on the number of terms for the vice president. The president, however, was barred from serving more than two terms.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-26) Under the provisions of these constitutions, only vice presidents Osmeña and Lopez have won re-election.

To date, only Fernando Lopez has served more than one term (a total of three terms), from 1949 to 1951, from 1965 to 1969, and again from 1969 until 1972 when the office was abolished. Under the 1987 Constitution, the vice president is barred from serving more than two consecutive terms (i.e. can be re-elected after one election cycle in between the last allowed term).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-:1-21)

### Impeachment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Impeachment")]

Impeachment in the Philippines follows procedures similar to the United States. The [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_the_Philippines "House of Representatives of the Philippines"), one of the houses of the bicameral Congress, has the exclusive power to initiate all cases of impeachment against the president, vice president, members of the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Supreme Court of the Philippines"), members of the Constitutional Commissions and the [ombudsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Ombudsman "Philippine Ombudsman"). When a third of its membership has endorsed the impeachment articles, it is then transmitted to the [Senate of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Philippines "Senate of the Philippines") which tries and decide, as impeachment tribunal, the impeachment case. A main difference from US proceedings however is that only a third of House members are required to approve the motion to impeach the president (as opposed to the majority required in the United States). In the Senate, selected members of the House of Representatives act as the prosecutors and the senators act as judges with the Senate president and chief justice of the Supreme Court jointly presiding over the proceedings. Like the United States, to convict the official in question requires that a minimum of two-thirds (i.e., 16 of 24 members) of the senate vote in favor of conviction. If an impeachment attempt is unsuccessful or the official is acquitted, no new cases can be filed against that impeachable official for at least one full year.

The Constitution enumerates the culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, and betrayal of public trust as grounds for the impeachment of the vice president, as applicable for the president, the members of the Supreme Court, the members of the Constitutional Commissions, and the ombudsman.

[Sara Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Duterte "Sara Duterte") is the first and only vice president in Philippine history to have been [impeached by the House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_impeachment_of_Sara_Duterte "First impeachment of Sara Duterte"). On February 5, 2025, 215 lawmakers signed the impeachment complaint against Duterte, with an additional 25 representatives signing a document the following day in support of the complaint, bringing the total to 240. Voting 19-4-1, the complaint had been "archived" by the Senate;[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-rappler_archv_imp-27) it is not yet clear if a trial could proceed later, in consideration of the pending motions for reconsideration before the Supreme Court.

### Vacancy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Vacancy")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/President_Arroyo_with_Vice_President_Teofisto_Guingona_%282003%29.jpg/250px-President_Arroyo_with_Vice_President_Teofisto_Guingona_%282003%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Arroyo_with_Vice_President_Teofisto_Guingona_(2003).jpg)

Vice President [Teofisto Guingona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teofisto_Guingona_Jr. "Teofisto Guingona Jr.") was appointed by President [Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Macapagal-Arroyo "Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo").

Section 9 of Article VII of the 1987 Philippines Constitution provides that whenever the office of vice president is vacant, the president shall nominate a vice president from among members of the Senate and House of Representatives, who shall assume office upon confirmation by a majority vote of all members of both houses of Congress, voting separately.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-Article_VII-15) When the vice president becomes the president by succession, the new president can nominate a member of the Congress subject to confirmation from the majority of all members of both houses of the Congress. The Senate president may not directly be in succession for the position of the vice presidency, unless nominated.

There is only one instance where a member of the Congress has assumed a vacancy in the vice president position, that is in the case of then-Senator [Teofisto Guingona Jr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teofisto_Guingona_Jr. "Teofisto Guingona Jr.")., who was appointed as vice president of the Philippines by Arroyo on February 7, 2001.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-28) Guingona is the only vice president not nationally elected to the position. He is also the oldest person to have held the position, being appointed at the age of 72. He also concurrently served as secretary of foreign affairs.

### Official residence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Official residence")]

Historically, the vice president was not given an official residence. However, the vice president also held office along with the president at the Executive Building (now Kalayaan Hall) in the complex of [Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace") from 1935 until 1972, when the position was abolished under martial law and the 1973 Constitution.

When the position was reinstated, Vice President [Salvador H. Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Laurel "Salvador Laurel") held office at the former Legislative Building on [Padre Burgos Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padre_Burgos_Avenue "Padre Burgos Avenue"), [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila"), until the building became the [National Museum of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Fine_Arts_(Manila) "National Museum of Fine Arts (Manila)") of the [National Museum of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_the_Philippines "National Museum of the Philippines"). The vice president's office was transferred to the [Philippine International Convention Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_International_Convention_Center "Philippine International Convention Center"), and again to the [PNB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_National_Bank "Philippine National Bank") Financial Center, both in [Pasay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasay "Pasay"), [Metro Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Manila "Metro Manila") in 2005.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-29) In 2011, the [Coconut Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_Palace "Coconut Palace"), also in [Pasay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasay "Pasay"), was designated as the principal workplace of the vice president of the Philippines. Beginning June 30, 2016, the office was transferred to the [Quezon City Reception House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_City_Reception_House "Quezon City Reception House") in [Quezon City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_City "Quezon City").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-30) In July 2022, the vice president's office was transferred to [Cybergate Plaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinsons_Cybergate "Robinsons Cybergate") in [Mandaluyong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandaluyong "Mandaluyong"), Metro Manila.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-33) Vice President [Sara Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Duterte "Sara Duterte") plans to establish a permanent office for the position.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-34)

### Travel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Travel")]

Vice presidents [Elpidio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino "Elpidio Quirino") and [Fernando Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Lopez "Fernando Lopez") used a 1946 [Packard Clipper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packard_Clipper "Packard Clipper").

The official state car of the Vice President of the Philippines from 1994 to 2016 was a [Mercedes-Benz W140 S-Class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_W140 "Mercedes-Benz W140"). [Jejomar Binay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jejomar_Binay "Jejomar Binay"), the Vice President between 2010 and 2016, used a bulletproof Toyota [Land Cruiser 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Land_Cruiser_(J200) "Toyota Land Cruiser (J200)") Series (which was replaced by the [LC 300 Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Land_Cruiser_(J300) "Toyota Land Cruiser (J300)") in 2022) or a Lexus [LX 570](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexus_LX_570 "Lexus LX 570") on some occasions.

The Vice President is also accompanied by a convoy of vehicles such as the Toyota [Innova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Innova "Toyota Innova"), [Hilux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Hilux "Toyota Hilux"), [Fortuner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Fortuner "Toyota Fortuner"), [HiAce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_HiAce "Toyota HiAce"), [Coaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Coaster "Toyota Coaster"), Land Cruisers, and Nissan Urvan, which contain personnel and security. In some instances, a [Toyota Sequoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Sequoia "Toyota Sequoia") was also utilized by Vice President Duterte.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-35)

Vice President Sara Duterte uses a [Sikorsky S-76C++](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikorsky_S-76 "Sikorsky S-76") helicopter. It has been criticized by some people, who argue that it is a waste of taxpayer money. However, the Vice President's office has defended the use of the helicopter, saying that it is necessary for her to travel quickly and safely around the country, and so she can visit her children anytime.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-37)

### Security

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Security")]

The Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSPG) is tasked with providing the vice president and his or her immediate family security throughout their term in office. Previously a separate unit, the VPSPG was put under the [Presidential Security Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Security_Command "Presidential Security Command") in 2024. Prior to the VPSPG's activation in 2022, the Vice Presidential Security Detachment (VPSD) was responsible for the security of the vice president, from [Salvador Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Laurel "Salvador Laurel") to [Leni Robredo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leni_Robredo "Leni Robredo").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-40) Similar to the setup of the PSC, the VPSPG's personnel jointly comes from the [Armed Forces of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_the_Philippines "Armed Forces of the Philippines") and the [Philippine National Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_National_Police "Philippine National Police").

As of November 2024, the VPSPG has a strength of 350 military and police personnel.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-41) In 2022, a Commission of Audit (COA) report revealed that the VPSPG had an initial strength of 433 personnel. By contrast, in 2020, the then-VPSD had a maximum of 83 personnel, before being reduced to 78 the following year.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-42)

## Post-vice presidency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vice_President_of_the_Philippines&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Post-vice presidency")]

Several vice presidents either lose re-election alongside their running mate or ascend to the presidency. After having been re-elected in 1941, Osmeña ascended to the presidency after President Quezon's death. Vice presidents Quirino and Garcia never ran for re-election as vice president as they would ascend to the presidency following the president's death. Vice president Lopez did not run for re-election in 1953, opting to run for senator instead. After being elected in 1998, Arroyo ascended to the presidency after President Estrada was ousted in the [Second EDSA Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_EDSA_Revolution "Second EDSA Revolution"). She later ran for re-election in 2004 and won. Five vice presidents ran for the presidency after their vice presidential term ended. Two of them, Macapagal in 1961 and Estrada in 1998 won. Three of them, Laurel in 1992, Binay in [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jejomar_Binay_2016_presidential_campaign "Jejomar Binay 2016 presidential campaign"), and Robredo in [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leni_Robredo_2022_presidential_campaign "Leni Robredo 2022 presidential campaign") lost.

Five vice presidents ran for another office after their vice presidential term ended and two succeeded. In 1953, Lopez ran and won for senator, finishing first. He would go on to win the vice presidency once more in 1965 and 1969. President Macapagal's running mate Pelaez also did not seek re-election for vice president, but instead sought the nomination of the opposing Nacionalista nomination for president, which he would eventually lose to then-senator Marcos.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines#cite_note-43) He would run for a seat in the House of Representatives in 1965 and won. In 2022, two vice presidents ran for senator; Binay lost, while de Castro withdrew less than a week after filing his candidacy. In 2025, Robredo ran for and won the position of Mayor of [Naga City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naga,_Camarines_Sur "Naga, Camarines Sur"). She is the first former vice president who did not later serve as president to run for and win a seat in a local executive position.

Only [Teofisto Guingona Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teofisto_Guingona_Jr. "Teofisto Guingona Jr.") did not pursue other office after his vice presidential term ended.

**Elpidio Rivera Quirino** (Tagalog:[[kiˈɾino]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Tagalog "Help:IPA/Tagalog"); November 16, 1890 – February 29, 1956) was the sixth [president of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines"), serving from 1948 to 1953. As the second [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines "Vice President of the Philippines") from 1946 to 1948, he assumed the presidency upon the death of [Manuel Roxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Roxas "Manuel Roxas") in 1948.

A lawyer by profession, Quirino entered politics when he became a representative of [Ilocos Sur's first district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Sur's_1st_congressional_district "Ilocos Sur's 1st congressional district") from 1919 to 1922. He was then elected as a senator from 1925 to 1935. In 1934, he became a member of the Philippine Independence Commission that was sent to [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), which secured the passage of [Tydings–McDuffie Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tydings%E2%80%93McDuffie_Act "Tydings–McDuffie Act") to the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Congress "American Congress"). In 1935, he was also elected to the [1935 Constitutional Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1934_Philippine_Constitutional_Convention_election "1934 Philippine Constitutional Convention election") that drafted the [1935 Philippine Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_Constitution_of_the_Philippines "1935 Constitution of the Philippines") for the newly established [Philippine Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_the_Philippines "Commonwealth of the Philippines"). In the new government, he served as secretary of the interior and finance under the cabinet of [President Manuel L. Quezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Quezon "Manuel Quezon").

After World War II, Quirino was elected vice-president in the [April 1946 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Philippine_general_election "1946 Philippine general election"), consequently the second and last for the Commonwealth and first for the [Third Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Republic_of_the_Philippines "Third Republic of the Philippines"). He won a full term under the [Liberal Party ticket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(Philippines) "Liberal Party (Philippines)"), defeating [Nacionalista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista "Nacionalista") former president [José P. Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_P._Laurel "José P. Laurel") as well as fellow _Liberalista_ and former [Senate President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_President_of_the_Philippines "Senate President of the Philippines")[José Dira Avelino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Avelino "José Avelino"). The Quirino administration was generally challenged by the Hukbalahap, who ransacked towns and barrios. Quirino ran for president again in November 1953 but was defeated by [Ramon Magsaysay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay "Ramon Magsaysay") in a landslide.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Elpidio_Quirino_at_UP_Class_1915.jpg/250px-Elpidio_Quirino_at_UP_Class_1915.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elpidio_Quirino_at_UP_Class_1915.jpg)

Quirino, Sabino Padilla, and [Jose P. Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_P._Laurel "Jose P. Laurel"), part of UP Class 1915, photographed in 1924

Elpidio Quirino y Rivera was born on November 16, 1890, at the [Vigan Provincial Jail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Sur_Provincial_Library "Ilocos Sur Provincial Library") in [Vigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigan "Vigan"), [Ilocos Sur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Sur_province "Ilocos Sur province"). He was the third child of Mariano Quirino y Quebral of [Caoayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caoayan "Caoayan"), Ilocos Sur and Gregoria Rivera y Mendoza of [Agoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agoo "Agoo"), [La Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Union "La Union").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-BM-1) A [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangley "Sangley")[mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_Mestizos "Filipino Mestizos") descendant, Quirino was baptized on November 19, 1890.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Tan_1986-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-3)

Quirino first attended secondary education at Vigan High School, during which he also worked as a teacher in barrio Caparia-an, Caoayan, Ilocos Sur. He later transferred to [Manila High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_High_School_(Intramuros) "Manila High School (Intramuros)") in [Intramuros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intramuros "Intramuros"), [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila"), after earning enough finances. He later studied law at the [University of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Philippines_Manila "University of the Philippines Manila"). He was one of the topnotchers of the 1915 [Philippine Bar Examinations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Bar_Examinations "Philippine Bar Examinations").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-4)

## Congressional career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Congressional career")]

### House of Representatives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: House of Representatives")]

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8c/Elpidio_Quirino_of_Ilocos_Sur%2C_Primer_Distrito_%281921%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elpidio_Quirino_of_Ilocos_Sur,_Primer_Distrito_(1921).jpg)

Elpidio Quirino as member of the House of Representatives, c.1921

Quirino was engaged in private law practice of until he was elected as member of the [Philippine House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_House_of_Representatives "Philippine House of Representatives") for [Ilocos Sur's 1st congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Sur's_1st_congressional_district "Ilocos Sur's 1st congressional district") from 1919 to 1922, succeeding Alberto Reyes. He served for only one term and was succeeded by Vicente Singson Pablo in 1922.

### Senate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Senate")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Honorable_Elpidio_Quirino_%28Delegates_from_the_Philippines%29.jpg/250px-Honorable_Elpidio_Quirino_%28Delegates_from_the_Philippines%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Honorable_Elpidio_Quirino_(Delegates_from_the_Philippines).jpg)

Quirino as a delegate to the Philippine Constitutional Convention, published by Benipayo Press (c.1935)

Quirino was first elected as a senator from the [1st senatorial district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines's_1st_senatorial_district "Philippines's 1st senatorial district") in 1925. He was re-elected in 1931 and served until the bicameral Congress was abolished in favor of the unicameral [National Assembly of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_the_Philippines "National Assembly of the Philippines").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:0-5)

As a senator, he was briefly assigned by Senate President [Manuel Quezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Quezon "Manuel Quezon") as acting [Senate Majority Leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_Floor_Leader_of_the_Senate_of_the_Philippines "Majority Floor Leader of the Senate of the Philippines") from 1932 to 1933[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:1-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:2-7) due to Quezon, senate majority leader [Benigno Aquino Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_Sr. "Benigno Aquino Sr."), and [Sergio Osmeña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Osme%C3%B1a "Sergio Osmeña") went on leave and made trips to the United States. These were to protect the proposed [Hare–Hawes–Cutting bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hare%E2%80%93Hawes%E2%80%93Cutting_Act "Hare–Hawes–Cutting Act") in U.S. Congress and to amend the bill because of opposition from the Philippine Legislature.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:1-6) In the senate, Quirino also became chairman of a joint committee on taxation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:2-7)

He was later secured a comeback to the Senate in 1941, but was not able to serve until 1945 due to [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:0-5) During the Philippine Commonwealth, he became Senate President pro tempore from 1942 but did not serve until 1945. His term as senator ended in 1946.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:0-5)

### Secretary of finance (1934 – 1936)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Secretary of finance (1934 – 1936)")]

In a memorandum to Governor General [Frank Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Murphy "Frank Murphy") on January 13, 1935, Quirino, quoting former acting finance secretary [Vicente Singson Encarnacion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Singson_Encarnacion "Vicente Singson Encarnacion"), proposed that the Philippines create its own currency system based on the gold standard. He supported this idea due to the country's gold production and simpler economic structure compared to the US and Europe. Quirino also agreed with Encarnacion on the need to devalue the [peso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_peso "Philippine peso"), suggesting a reduction aligned with previous currency changes in 1934. He recommended forming a [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank") to stabilize prices and promote the national economy, over which he emphasized its role in lowering interest rates and expanding credit. However, Quirino's proposals, like those of his predecessor, were not adopted. The [Philippine Insular government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insular_Government_of_the_Philippine_Islands "Insular Government of the Philippine Islands") enacted Act No. 4199 on March 16, 1935, fixing the peso to the US dollar, marking the official introduction of the dollar exchange standard.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-8):102

## Vice presidency (1946–1948)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Vice presidency (1946–1948)")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Official_Portrait_of_Vice_President_Elpidio_Quirino%2C_1947_%282%29.jpg/250px-Official_Portrait_of_Vice_President_Elpidio_Quirino%2C_1947_%282%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Official_Portrait_of_Vice_President_Elpidio_Quirino,_1947_(2).jpg)

Photograph from the _Blue Book: First Anniversary of the Republic of the Philippines_, published 1947

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Elpidio_Quirino_during_Manuel_Roxas_wake.jpg/250px-Elpidio_Quirino_during_Manuel_Roxas_wake.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elpidio_Quirino_during_Manuel_Roxas_wake.jpg)

President Elpidio Quirino weeps beside the coffin of his predecessor, Manuel Roxas during the latter's wake in 1948

Soon after the reconstitution of the Commonwealth government in 1945, Senators [Manuel Roxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Roxas "Manuel Roxas"), Quirino and their allies called for an early national election to choose the president and vice president of the Philippines and members of the Congress. In December 1945, the House Insular Affairs of the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") approved the joint resolution setting the date of the election on not later than April 30, 1946.

Prompted by this congressional action, President [Sergio Osmeña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergio_Osme%C3%B1a "Sergio Osmeña") called the [Philippine Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Philippines "Congress of the Philippines") to a three-day special session. Congress enacted Commonwealth Act No. 725, setting the date of the election on April 23, 1946. The act was signed by President Osmeña on January 5, 1946.

Quirino was nominated as Senate President [Manuel Roxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Roxas "Manuel Roxas")'s running mate. The tandem won the election. As Vice President, Quirino was appointed Secretary of Foreign Affairs.
