Quirino's five years as president were marked by notable postwar reconstruction, general economic gains and increased economic aid from the United States.

### Administration and cabinet

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Administration and cabinet")]

Main article: [List of cabinets of the Philippines §Elpidio Quirino (1948–1953)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cabinets_of_the_Philippines#Elpidio_Quirino_(1948%E2%80%931953) "List of cabinets of the Philippines")

### First term (1948–1949)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: First term (1948–1949)")]

#### Accession

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Accession")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Qurinoinugration1948.jpg/250px-Qurinoinugration1948.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Qurinoinugration1948.jpg)

Vice President Quirino taking the oath of office as inaugurated as President of the Philippines at the Council of State Room, Executive Building, [Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace").

Quirino assumed the presidency on April 17, 1948, taking his oath of office two days after the death of Manuel Roxas two days earlier of a heart attack after delivering a speech at [Clark Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Air_Base "Clark Air Base") in [Pampanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampanga "Pampanga"). The inauguration took place at the Council of State Room of the Malacañang Palace in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila") as the second non-scheduled extraordinary [presidential inauguration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_presidential_inauguration "Philippine presidential inauguration").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-9)[Associate Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associate_Justice_of_the_Philippines "Associate Justice of the Philippines") of the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Supreme Court of the Philippines")[Ricardo Paras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Paras "Ricardo Paras") administered the oath of office. On the same day, Quirino delivered his short, 47-word inaugural remarks at the same room.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-10)

His first official act as the President was the proclamation of a [state mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_funeral "State funeral") throughout the country for Roxas's death. Since Quirino was a widower, his surviving daughter, Victoria, would serve as the official hostess and perform the functions traditionally ascribed to the [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_Philippines "First Lady of the Philippines").

#### New capital city

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: New capital city")]

On July 17, 1948, Congress approved Republic Act No. 333, amending Commonwealth Act No. 502, declaring [Quezon City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_City "Quezon City") as the new capital of the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"), replacing [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) Nevertheless, pending the official transfer of the government offices to the new capital site, Manila remained to be such for all effective purposes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

#### Hukbalahap

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Hukbalahap")]

The term Hukbalahap was a contraction of _Hukbo ng Bayan Laban sa mga Hapon_ (in English: The Nation's Army Against the Japanese [Soldiers]), members of which were commonly referred to as _Huks_.

With the expiration of the Amnesty deadline on August 15, 1948, the government found out that the [Huks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hukbalahap "Hukbalahap") had not lived up to the terms of the Quirino-Taruc agreement. Indeed, after having been seated in Congress and collecting his back pay allowance, Huk leader [Luis Taruc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Taruc "Luis Taruc") surreptitiously fled away from Manila, even as a number of his followers had either submitted themselves to the conditions of the Amnesty proclamation or surrendered their arms. In the face of countercharges from the Huk to the effect that the government had not satisfied the agreed conditions, President Quirino ordered a stepped-up campaign against dissidents, restoring once more an aggressive policy in view of the failure of the friendly attitude previously adopted.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

#### Fireside chats

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Fireside chats")]

To bring the government closer to the people, he revived President Quezon's "fireside chats", in which he enlightened the people on the activities of the Republic by the periodic radio broadcasts from Malacañang Palace.

#### Impeachment attempt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Impeachment attempt")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Quirino-waving.jpg/250px-Quirino-waving.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quirino-waving.jpg)

Quirino waving to the crowd

Riding on the crest of the growing wave of resentment against the Liberal Party, a move was next hatched to indict President Quirino himself.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) Led by Representative Agripino Escareal, a committee composed of seven members of the House of Representatives prepared a five-count accusation ranging from [nepotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism") to gross expenditures. [Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_House_of_Representatives_of_the_Philippines "Speaker of the House of Representatives of the Philippines") Eugenio Pérez appointed a committee of seven, headed by Representative [Lorenzo Sumulong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenzo_Sumulong "Lorenzo Sumulong") to look into the charges preparatory to their filing with the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Philippines "Senate of the Philippines"), acting as an impeachment body. [Solicitor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Solicitor_General_(Philippines) "Office of the Solicitor General (Philippines)") Felix Angelo Bautista entered his appearance as defense counsel for the chief executive.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) Following several hearings, on April 19, 1949, after a rather turbulent session that lasted all night, the congressional committee reached a verdict completely exonerating the President.

#### Romulo becomes President of the UN General Assembly

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Romulo becomes President of the UN General Assembly")]

In September 1949, the Fourth General Assembly of the United Nations elected delegate [Carlos P. Romulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_P._Romulo "Carlos P. Romulo") as its [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_Nations_General_Assembly "President of the United Nations General Assembly"). The first[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) Oriental to hold the position, Romulo was strongly supported by the [Anglo-Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon "Anglo-Saxon") bloc, as well as by the group of Spanish-speaking nations,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) thus underscoring the hybrid nature of the Filipino people's culture and upbringing.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

#### 1949 presidential election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: 1949 presidential election")]

Main article: [1949 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Philippine_presidential_election "1949 Philippine presidential election")

Incumbent President Quirino won a full term as president after the untimely death of President Manuel Roxas in 1948 in the [November 1949 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Philippine_presidential_election "1949 Philippine presidential election"). His running mate, [Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Philippines "Senate of the Philippines")[Fernando López](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_L%C3%B3pez "Fernando López"), won as [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines "Vice President of the Philippines"). Despite factions created in the administration party, Quirino won a satisfactory vote from the public. It was the only time in Philippine history where the duly elected president, vice president and senators all came from the same party, the Liberal Party. The election was widely criticized as being corrupt,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-12) with violence and fraud taking place.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-13) Opponents of Quirino were beaten or murdered by his supporters or the police and the election continues to be seen as corrupt.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-14)

### Second term (1949–1953)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Second term (1949–1953)")]

Quirino's second inauguration took place on Friday, December 30, 1949, at the [Independence Grandstand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_Grandstand "Quirino Grandstand") in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-15)[Chief Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_Philippines "Chief Justice of the Philippines") of the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Supreme Court of the Philippines")[Manuel Moran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Moran "Manuel Moran") administered the oath of office.

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Quirino1949Inauguration.jpg/250px-Quirino1949Inauguration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quirino1949Inauguration.jpg)

President Elpidio Quirino taking the oath of office for his first full term as President of the Philippines at the Independence Grandstand (now [Quirino Grandstand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_Grandstand "Quirino Grandstand")) in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila").

#### Regional conference

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Regional conference")]

In May 1950, upon the invitation of President Quirino and through the insistent suggestion of United Nations General Assembly President Romulo, official representatives of [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan"), [Ceylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sri_Lanka "Sri Lanka"), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand"), [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia"), and [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") met in [Baguio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baguio "Baguio") for a regional conference sponsored by the Philippines.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)[Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") and [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea") did not attend the conference because the latter did not contemplate the formation of a military union of the [Southeast Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") nations. On the other hand, Japan, Indonesia, Taiwan, and others were not invited because, at the time, they were not free and independent states.[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Elpidio\_Quirino#Dubious "Talk:Elpidio Quirino")_] Due to the request of India and Indonesia, no political questions were taken up the conference.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) Instead, the delegates discussed economic and, most of all, cultural, problems confronting their respective countries. Strangely enough however, the Baguio Conference ended with an official [communiqué](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communiqu%C3%A9 "Communiqué") in which the nations attending the same expressed their united agreement in supporting the right to self-determination of all peoples the world over. This initial regional meet held much promise of a future alliance of these neighboring nations for common protection and aid.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

#### Huks' continued re-insurgence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Huks' continued re-insurgence")]

The Quirino administration faced a serious threat in the form of the [communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism "Communism") Hukbalahap movement. Although the Huks originally had been an anti-Japanese guerrilla army in Luzon, communists steadily gained control over the leadership, and when Quirino's negotiation with Huk commander Luis Taruc broke down in 1948. Taruc then openly declared himself a communist and called for the overthrow of the government.

#### Peace campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Peace campaign")]

With the communist organization estimated to still have more than 40,000 duly registered members by March 1951, the government went on with its sustained campaign to cope with the worsening peace and order problem.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) The 1951 budget included the use of a residue fund for the land resettlement program in favor of the surrendered HUKS. The money helped maintain the Economic Development Corps (EDCOR), with its settlements of 6,500 hectares in Kapatagan ([Lanao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanao_(province) "Lanao (province)")) and 25,000 hectares in Buldon ([Cotabato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotabato "Cotabato")). In each group taken to these places there was a nucleus of former Army personnel and their families, who became a stabilizing factor and ensured the success of the program. Indeed, less than ten percent of the Huks who settled down gave up this new lease in life offered them by the government.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

To promote the smooth restructuring of the [Armed Forces of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_the_Philippines "Armed Forces of the Philippines"), the military were made to undergo a reorganization.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) Battalion combat teams of 1,000 men each were established. Each operated independently of the High Command, except for overall coordination in operational plans. A total of 26 Battalion Combat Teams were put up. New army units were also established, such was the first [Airborne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airborne_forces "Airborne forces") Unit, the [Scout Rangers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Scout_Ranger_Regiment "1st Scout Ranger Regiment"), the [Canine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog "Dog") Unit, and the [Cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry") Unit. These units all showed considerable ability.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

#### Assassination plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Assassination plot")]

In early January 1951, a communist plot to assassinate leading government officials was discovered following the seizure of documents in a rebel camp, which showed that 40 men had been hired for the plan.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-dm0151t-16) Among the intended victims were Quirino, Lopez, and then defense secretary Magsaysay.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-dm0151t-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-ma0151t-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-gb0151g-18) On January 24, four [Chinese nationals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_people "Chinese people")—suspected would-be assassins—were arrested in a raid in [Chinatown, Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinatown,_Manila "Chinatown, Manila");[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-dm0151t-16)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-gb0151g-18) they were later held at [Philippine Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Army "Philippine Army") headquarters at [Camp Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Aguinaldo "Camp Aguinaldo").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-gb0151g-18)

Intelligence sources reported that the plot was directed by Co Pak, a businessman who had been arrested[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-ma0151t-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-gb0151g-18) for allegedly supporting the Hukbalahap and his fellow communists in the country.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-cma0251t-19) He had escaped every arrests several times. On February 19, he was [deported](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deport "Deport") by the government to [Formosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formosa "Formosa") through a [Philippine Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Air_Force "Philippine Air Force") plane.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-cma0251t-19)

#### 1951 midterm election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: 1951 midterm election")]

Main article: [1951 Philippine general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951_Philippine_general_election "1951 Philippine general election")

After a sweep by the Liberals in 1949, many Filipinos doubted the election result. This brought a sweep by the [Nacionalistas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista_Party "Nacionalista Party") in the 1951 elections. There was a special election for the vacated Senate seat of [Fernando Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Lopez "Fernando Lopez"), who won as vice president in 1949. The Liberals won no seats in the Senate.

#### 1953 presidential election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: 1953 presidential election")]

Main article: [1953 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Philippine_presidential_election "1953 Philippine presidential election")

Quirino ran for re-election to the presidency with [José Yulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Yulo "José Yulo") as his running mate in 1953 despite his ill health. His [Secretary of National Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_National_Defense_(Philippines) "Department of National Defense (Philippines)"), [Ramon Magsaysay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay "Ramon Magsaysay"), resigned from office and joined the [Nacionalista Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista_Party "Nacionalista Party"). Other prominent [Liberals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(Philippines) "Liberal Party (Philippines)") including Vice President Fernando Lopez, Ambassador Carlos Romulo, and Senators [Tomás Cabili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom%C3%A1s_Cabili "Tomás Cabili") and [Juan Sumulong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Sumulong "Juan Sumulong") also bolted Quirino's party.

On August 22, 1953, the [Nacionalista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista_Party "Nacionalista Party") and [Democratic Parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(Philippines) "Democratic Party (Philippines)") formed a coalition to ensure Quirino's full defeat. On [Election Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Philippine_presidential_election "1953 Philippine presidential election"), Quirino was defeated by Magsaysay with a landslide vote margin of 1.5 million.

Quirino was accused of a [Golden arinola scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_arinola_scandal "Golden arinola scandal") which led him to losing the [1953 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Philippine_presidential_election "1953 Philippine presidential election").

#### Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Economy")]

Upon assuming the reins of government, Quirino announced two main objectives of his administration: first, the [economic reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_reconstruction "Economic reconstruction") of the nation and second, the restoration of the faith and confidence of the people in the government. In connection to the first agenda, he created the President's Action Committee on Social Amelioration (PACSA) to mitigate the sufferings of indigent families, the Labor Management Advisory Board to advise him on labor matters, the Agricultural Credit Cooperatives Financing Administration (ACCFA) to help the farmers market their crops and save them from loan sharks, and the Rural Banks of the Philippines to facilitate credit utilities in rural areas.

The Import and Exchange Control Act of 1948 was fully implemented only after Quirino won. During his term, Congress also created the [Central Bank of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangko_Sentral_ng_Pilipinas "Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas") to control currency, banking, and credit. Before implementing controls, the Bell Trade Act required approval from the U. S. President. President [Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman") agreed to the controls if the Philippines accepted an all-American economic mission called the Bell Mission, led by [Daniel Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Bell "Daniel Bell"), which surveyed the country's economy in July 1950. The mission reported the harsh economic conditions of the Philippines. Its findings led to the Romulo-Snyder Agreement and the Quirino-Foster Agreement, including a $70 million loan proposal from Central Bank Governor [Miguel Cuaderno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cuaderno_Sr. "Miguel Cuaderno Sr.").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:3-20)

#### Social programs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Social programs")]

Enhancing President Manuel Roxas' policy of social justice to alleviate the lot of the common mass, President Quirino, almost immediately after assuming office, started a series of steps calculated to effectively ameliorate the economic condition of the people.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) After periodic surprise visits to the slums of Manila and other backward regions of the country, President Quirino officially made public a seven-point program for social security which included the following:[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

1.   Unemployment insurance
2.   Old-age insurance
3.   Accident and permanent disability insurance
4.   Health insurance
5.   Maternity insurance
6.   State relief; and
7.   Labor opportunities

President Quirino also created the Social Security Commission and appointed Social Welfare Commissioner Asuncion Perez as its chairperson.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) This was followed by the creation of the PACSA, charges with extending aid, loans, and relief to less fortunate citizens. Both the policy and its implementation were hailed by the people as harbingers of great benefits.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

#### Agrarian reform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Agrarian reform")]

See also: [Land reform in the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_the_Philippines "Land reform in the Philippines")

As part of his agrarian reform agenda, President Quirino issued Executive Order No. 355 on October 23, 1950, which replaced the National Land Settlement Administration with Land Settlement Development Corporation (LASEDECO) which takes over the responsibilities of the Agricultural Machinery Equipment Corporation and the Rice and Corn Production Administration.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-21)

#### Integrity board

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Integrity board")]

Following calls for government improvement from Vice President Fernando Lopez, President Quirino created the Integrity Board to probe into reports of graft and corruption in high government positions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

### Foreign policies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Foreign policies")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/Truman_Quirino.jpg/250px-Truman_Quirino.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Truman_Quirino.jpg)

US President [Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman") in the Oval Office, evidently receiving a cane as a gift from the Philippine President Elpidio Quirino as Ambassador [Joaquín Elizalde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joaqu%C3%ADn_Miguel_Elizalde "Joaquín Miguel Elizalde") looks on.

Quirino's administration excelled in diplomacy, impressing foreign heads of states and world statesmen by his intelligence and culture. He had official travels to the United States, European countries, and Southeast Asia. During his six years in office, he and his [Foreign Affairs Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_minister "Foreign minister"), [Helen Cutaran Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Anthony_Cutaran_Bennett "Roy Anthony Cutaran Bennett"), was able to negotiate treaties and agreements with other nations of the [Free World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_World "Free World"). Two Asian heads of state visited the country—President [Chiang Kai-shek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiang_Kai-shek "Chiang Kai-shek") of the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") in July 1949 and President [Sukarno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukarno "Sukarno") of [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia") in January 1951.

In 1950, at the onset of the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War"), President Quirino authorized the deployment of over 7,450 Filipino soldiers to Korea, under the designation of the [Philippine Expeditionary Forces to Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Expeditionary_Forces_to_Korea "Philippine Expeditionary Forces to Korea") (PEFTOK).

> While I recognise the United States as a great builder in this country, I have never surrendered the sovereignty, much less the dignity and future of our country.

—Elpidio Quirino[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-quirino-phil-arch-22)

In 1951, the Philippines signed the [Mutual Defense Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_Defense_Treaty_(United_States%E2%80%93Philippines) "Mutual Defense Treaty (United States–Philippines)") with the United States to deter the threat of [communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism "Communism") that existed during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"). The military alliance remains to this day a key pillar of American foreign policy in Asia that also includes defense pacts with Japan, South Korea, Thailand, and Australia.

In an apparent show of genuine forgiveness and an attempt to improve public relations with Japan, Quirino granted amnesty to all Japanese war criminals and Filipino collaborators who were serving time or on death row in the Philippines. Quirino had lost his own wife and three children to the Japanese, along with five other members of his family. Despite this great personal loss, he said, "I do not want my children and my people to inherit from me hate for people who might yet be our friends, for the permanent interest of the country."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-IAFOR2016-23) Due to the high anti-Japanese sentiment at the time, many observers considered his actions to be political suicide.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-IAFOR2016-23) Controversially, Quirino even pardoned Japanese war criminals who murdered, raped, and inflicted other serious crimes towards Filipinos during World War II. The _[Manila Bulletin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila\_Bulletin "Manila Bulletin")_, an influential Filipino newspaper, has described his actions as "a historic gesture of 'forgiving the unforgivable'".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-MB2023-24) All of the convicts were released by December 1953. They had been tried by the American-operated [Philippine War Crimes Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_War_Crimes_Commission "Philippine War Crimes Commission") or Filipino civil courts.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-25) The pardons contributed to the reconciliation between the Philippines and Japan which eventually led to a friendly relationship.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-PNA2023-26)

#### Korean War

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Korean War")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Vicky_Quirino_%28Malacanang_photo%29.jpg/250px-Vicky_Quirino_%28Malacanang_photo%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vicky_Quirino_(Malacanang_photo).jpg)

His daughter [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Quirino-Gonzalez "Victoria Quirino-Gonzalez") served as the First Lady during his presidency

On June 25, 1950, the world was astonished to hear the [North Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea") aggression against the independent South Korea. The United Nations immediately took up this challenge to the security of this part of the world. Carlos Romulo soon stood out as the most effective spokesman for the South Korean cause.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) On behalf of the government, Romulo offered to send a Philippine military contingent to be under the overall command of General [Douglas MacArthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_MacArthur "Douglas MacArthur"), who had been named United Nations supreme commander for the punitive expedition. The Philippines, thus, became the first country to join the United States in the offer of military assistance to beleaguered South Korea.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

President Quirino took the necessary steps to make the Philippine offer. On a purely voluntary basis, the first contingent – the Tenth Battalion Combat Team – was formed under Colonel Azurin, and dispatched to Korea, where its members quickly won much renown for their military skill and bravery. The name of Captain Jose Artiaga Jr., heroically killed in action, stands out as a symbol of the country's contribution to the cause of freedom outside native shores. Other Philippine Combat Teams successively replaced the first contingent sent, and they all built a name for discipline, tenacity, and courage, until the armistice that brought the conflict to a halt.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

#### Quirino-Foster Agreement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Quirino-Foster Agreement")]

By the time of the creation of the Integrity Board, the Bell Mission, led by American banker [Daniel W. Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_W._Bell "Daniel W. Bell") and composed of five members with a staff of twenty workers, following their period of stay in the Philippines, beginning in July 1950, finally submitted its report on October of the same year.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) The report made several proposals, most noteworthy, of which were that the United States on, President Quirino gamely and patriotically,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11) took in the recommendations and sought to implement them. Thus, in November 1950, President Quirino and [William Chapman Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Chapman_Foster "William Chapman Foster"), representing the [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government "United States government"), signed an agreement by virtue of which the former pledged to obtain the necessary Philippine legislation, in keeping with the Bell Mission Report, while envoy Foster promised the necessary by the same report.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-Molina_1961-11)

The agreement also called for renegotiating the Bell Trade Agreement and signing a Treaty of Friendship, Commerce, and Navigation for the U.S. recognition of the Philippines’ independence. Senator [Claro M. Recto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claro_M._Recto "Claro M. Recto") labeled this a “mendicant foreign policy” since it allowed U.S. advisors into government offices, leading to official American intervention in the country's government and economy.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-:3-20)

However, much as he tried to become a good president, Quirino failed to win the people's affection. Several factors caused the unpopularity of his administration, namely:[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-27)

*   Failure of the government to check the Huk threat that made travel in the provinces unsafe, as evidenced by the killing of former [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_Philippines "First Lady of the Philippines")[Aurora Quezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora_Quezon "Aurora Quezon") and her companions on April 28, 1949, by the Huks on the Bongabong-Baler Road in Baler, Tayabas (now part of [Aurora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora_(province) "Aurora (province)"));
*   Economic distress of the times, aggravated by rising unemployment rate, soaring prices of commodities, and unfavorable balance of trade.

#### Executive clemency to Japanese war criminals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Executive clemency to Japanese war criminals")]

On July 4, 1953, during the final year of his presidency, Quirino made a historic and controversial act of clemency by granting pardons to 114 [Japanese prisoners of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_prisoners_of_war_in_World_War_II "Japanese prisoners of war in World War II") who had been convicted for atrocities committed during the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), including acts perpetrated during the [Japanese occupation of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_occupation_of_the_Philippines "Japanese occupation of the Philippines"). Many of these prisoners had been held at the [New Bilibid Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bilibid_Prison "New Bilibid Prison") in Muntinlupa.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-28)

Quirino, whose own wife, three of his children, and several relatives had been killed by Japanese forces during the [Battle of Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Manila_(1945) "Battle of Manila (1945)"), explained that his decision was driven by a desire for reconciliation and peace in the region. He stated that he bore no personal hatred and hoped the gesture would promote healing and foster improved relations between the Philippines and Japan.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-29)

Alongside the clemency for Japanese war criminals, President Quirino also granted amnesty to 323 Filipinos who had been convicted of collaboration with the Japanese during the occupation. These collaborators had either held positions in the wartime [Second Philippine Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Philippine_Republic "Second Philippine Republic") or had supported Japanese military operations in various capacities.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-30)

The dual acts of clemency were received with mixed reactions—praised by some as a magnanimous step towards forgiveness and criticised by others as a betrayal of the memory of wartime suffering. Nonetheless, Quirino's actions laid a foundation for [post-war diplomatic normalisation with Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan%E2%80%93Philippines_relations "Japan–Philippines relations") and signalled a commitment to national healing.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-31)

## Post-presidency and death (1953–1956)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Post-presidency and death (1953–1956)")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/President_Quirino.jpg/250px-President_Quirino.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Quirino.jpg)

Quirino in his mid 60s

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/2671Taguig_City_Landmarks_39.jpg/250px-2671Taguig_City_Landmarks_39.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2671Taguig_City_Landmarks_39.jpg)

The present tomb of Elpidio Quirino at the [Libingan ng mga Bayani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libingan_ng_mga_Bayani "Libingan ng mga Bayani").

Following his failed bid for re-election, Quirino retired to private life. He offered his dedication to serve the Filipino people, becoming the "Father of [Foreign Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_service "Diplomatic service")" in the Philippines.

In the evening of February 29, 1956, Quirino was preparing to attend a meeting when he suffered a massive heart attack. He died shortly thereafter at 6:35 pm, at the age of 65, at his retirement house in [Novaliches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novaliches "Novaliches"), Quezon City. President [Ramon Magsaysay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay "Ramon Magsaysay") later declared March 1 to 15 as a "[period of national mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_day_of_mourning "National day of mourning")", wherein all flags at all government establishments in the country were flown at half-mast as a sign of mourning.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-32) Quirino's remains lay in state at the [Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace") from March 2 to 4. On March 5, a necrological service was held for him at the [Legislative Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Fine_Arts_(Manila) "National Museum of Fine Arts (Manila)") in Manila and his remains were later interred at the [Manila South Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_South_Cemetery "Manila South Cemetery").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-34)

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Manila_South_Cemetery_graves_Manila_%28Metro_Manila%3B_2023-08-18%29_E911a_06.jpg/250px-Manila_South_Cemetery_graves_Manila_%28Metro_Manila%3B_2023-08-18%29_E911a_06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manila_South_Cemetery_graves_Manila_(Metro_Manila;_2023-08-18)_E911a_06.jpg)

Quirino's tomb at Manila South Cemetery.

On February 29, 2016, his remains were relocated and reinterred at a special tomb site in the [Libingan ng mga Bayani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libingan_ng_mga_Bayani "Libingan ng mga Bayani") in [Taguig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taguig "Taguig"), in time for the 60th anniversary of his death.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-35)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Personal life")]

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Quirino_Family_before_World_War_II.jpg/250px-Quirino_Family_before_World_War_II.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Quirino_Family_before_World_War_II.jpg)

Quirino's family before [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II")

Quirino was married to [Alicia Syquía](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alicia_Syquia "Alicia Syquia") (1903–1945) on January 16, 1921. The couple had five children: Tomás, Armando, Norma, [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Quirino-Gonzalez "Victoria Quirino-Gonzalez"), and Fe Angela. On February 9, 1945, his wife and three of their children (Armando, Norma and Fe Angela) were killed by Japanese troops as they fled their home during the [Battle of Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Manila_(1945) "Battle of Manila (1945)").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-36) His brother [Antonio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Quirino "Antonio Quirino") was the owner of Alto Broadcasting System, which later merged with Chronicle Broadcasting Network to form the [ABS-CBN Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABS-CBN_Broadcasting_Corporation "ABS-CBN Broadcasting Corporation").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-37)

His daughter, [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Quirino-Delgado "Victoria Quirino-Delgado"), became the youngest hostess of [Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace"), at 16 years old, when Quirino ascended to the presidency on April 17, 1948. She married Luis M. Gonzalez in 1950, who became [Philippine ambassador to Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_Philippines_to_Spain "List of ambassadors of the Philippines to Spain") from 1966 to 1971.

## Memorials

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Elpidio_Quirino&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Memorials")]

There are a number of memorials dedicated to Quirino. In 1964, the municipality of Angaki in Ilocos Sur was renamed to [Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino,_Ilocos_Sur "Quirino, Ilocos Sur") in his honor.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-41) The province of [Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino "Quirino"), established in 1966, was named in his memory. Newer municipalities named after him, such as [Quirino, Isabela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino,_Isabela "Quirino, Isabela") and [President Quirino, Sultan Kudarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Quirino,_Sultan_Kudarat "President Quirino, Sultan Kudarat"), were later established in 1967 and 1973, respectively.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-43) Streets like the [Quirino Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_Avenue "Quirino Avenue") in Manila and [Elpidio Quirino Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino_Avenue "Elpidio Quirino Avenue") in [Parañaque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Para%C3%B1aque "Parañaque") are named for him. The Novaliches–Ipo Road, where his retirement home is situated, was renamed as [Quirino Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_Highway "Quirino Highway"). The Independence Grandstand in Manila's [Rizal Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_Park "Rizal Park") was also renamed to [Quirino Grandstand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_Grandstand "Quirino Grandstand") in his honor.

Once the [Quirino Avenue station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_station_(MRT) "Quirino station (MRT)") of [MRT Line 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MRT_Line_7 "MRT Line 7") and the [Quirino Highway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_Highway_station "Quirino Highway station") of the [Metro Manila Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Manila_Subway "Metro Manila Subway") commence operations, Quirino will have three train stations named after him, including the [Quirino station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_station_(LRT) "Quirino station (LRT)") of [LRT Line 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LRT_Line_1 "LRT Line 1").

In 2016, a memorial to him was established in [Hibiya Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibiya_Park "Hibiya Park"), Tokyo, Japan.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-46)

Yearly on November 16, special holidays in commemoration of his birth are observed at his home province of [Ilocos Sur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Sur "Ilocos Sur") and [La Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Union "La Union"), respectively.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino#cite_note-48)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

President of the Philippines from 1953 to 1957

"Magsaysay" redirects here. For other uses, see [Magsaysay (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magsaysay_(disambiguation) "Magsaysay (disambiguation)").

In this [Filipino name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_name "Filipino name"), the [middle name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_name "Middle name") or maternal [family name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surname "Surname") is _del Fierro_ and the surname or paternal family name is _Magsaysay_.

**Ramon del Fierro Magsaysay Sr.**[QSC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_Service_Cross "Quezon Service Cross")[GCGH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Golden_Heart_(Philippines) "Order of the Golden Heart (Philippines)")[KGE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_White_Elephant "Order of the White Elephant")[GCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Grand_Cross_Royal_Order_of_Cambodia "Knight Grand Cross Royal Order of Cambodia") (August 31, 1907 – March 17, 1957) was a Filipino politician and military officer who was the seventh [president of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines"), serving from 1953 until [his death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957_Cebu_Douglas_C-47_crash "1957 Cebu Douglas C-47 crash") in 1957. An automobile mechanic by profession, Magsaysay was appointed military governor of Zambales after serving as a guerrilla leader during the [Pacific War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_War "Pacific War"). He then served two terms as [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(Philippines) "Liberal Party (Philippines)") congressman for [Zambales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambales "Zambales")'s [at-large district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambales's_at-large_congressional_district "Zambales's at-large congressional district") before being appointed Secretary of National Defense by President [Elpidio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino "Elpidio Quirino"). He was eventually elected as president under the banner of the [Nacionalista Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista_Party "Nacionalista Party"), the youngest to be elected to the position, and second youngest overall (after [Emilio Aguinaldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Aguinaldo "Emilio Aguinaldo")). He was the first Philippine president born in the 20th century and the first to be born after the [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire")[colonial era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Philippines_(1521%E2%80%931898) "History of the Philippines (1521–1898)"). Magsaysay died in a plane crash on March 17, 1957, in [Cebu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cebu "Cebu"). His successor, [Carlos P. Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_P._Garcia "Carlos P. Garcia"), assumed the presidency. He is the most recent Philippine president to have died in office.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Ramon_Magsaysay_teenager.jpg/250px-Ramon_Magsaysay_teenager.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ramon_Magsaysay_teenager.jpg)

Magsaysay in his teenage years

Ramon del Fierro Magsaysay, of mixed [Tagalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagalog_people "Tagalog people"), [Visayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visayans "Visayans"), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards "Spaniards"), and [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangley "Sangley") descent,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-5) was born in [Iba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iba,_Zambales "Iba, Zambales") on August 31, 1907, to Exequiel Magsaysay y de los Santos (April 18, 1874, in [San Marcelino, Zambales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Marcelino,_Zambales "San Marcelino, Zambales") – January 24, 1969, in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila")), a blacksmith, and Perfecta del Fierro y Quimson (April 18, 1886, in [Castillejos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castillejos "Castillejos"), Zambales – May 5, 1981, in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila")), a [Chinese mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangley "Sangley") schoolteacher, nurse.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Reader's_Digest-6)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-:0-4)

He spent his grade school life somewhere in Castillejos and his high school life at Zambales Academy in [San Narciso, Zambales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Narciso,_Zambales "San Narciso, Zambales").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-BureauOfPrinting-1950-7) After college, Magsaysay entered the [University of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Philippines "University of the Philippines") in 1927,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-BureauOfPrinting-1950-7) where he enrolled in a Mechanical Engineering course. He first worked as a chauffeur to support himself as he studied engineering; and later, he transferred to the Institute of Commerce at José Rizal College (now [José Rizal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Rizal_University "José Rizal University")) from 1928 to 1932,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-BureauOfPrinting-1950-7) where he received a [baccalaureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in commerce. He then worked as an automobile mechanic for a bus company[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Greenberg-1987-8) and shop superintendent.

### Career during World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career during World War II")]

At the outbreak of World War II, he joined the motor pool of the 31st Infantry Division of the [Philippine Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Army "Philippine Army"). When [Bataan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataan "Bataan") surrendered in 1942, Magsaysay escaped to the hills, narrowly evading Japanese arrest on at least four occasions. There he organised the Western Luzon Guerrilla Forces, and was commissioned captain on April 5, 1942. For three years, Magsaysay operated under Col. [Frank Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Merrill "Frank Merrill")'s famed guerrilla outfit and saw action at Sawang, San Marcelino, Zambales, first as a supply officer codenamed _Chow_ and later as commander of a 10,000-strong force.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Reader's_Digest-6)

Magsaysay was among those instrumental in clearing the Zambales coast of the Japanese prior to the landing of American forces together with [Philippine Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Commonwealth "Philippine Commonwealth") troops on January 29, 1945.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Family")]

He was married to [Luz Rosauro Banzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luz_Magsaysay "Luz Magsaysay") on June 16, 1933, and they had three children: Teresita (1934–1979), Milagros (b. 1936) and [Ramon Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay,_Jr. "Ramon Magsaysay, Jr.") (b. 1938).

Several of Magsaysay's relatives became prominent public figures in their own right:

*   [Ramon "Jun" Banzon Magsaysay Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay_Jr. "Ramon Magsaysay Jr."), son; former Congressman and Senator
*   Francisco "Paco" Delgado Magsaysay, entrepreneur
*   [Genaro Magsaysay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genaro_Magsaysay "Genaro Magsaysay"), brother; former Senator
*   [Vicente Magsaysay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Magsaysay "Vicente Magsaysay"), nephew; Former Governor of [Zambales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambales "Zambales")
*   [JB Magsaysay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JB_Magsaysay "JB Magsaysay"), grandnephew; actor, politician, and businessman
*   [Antonio Magsaysay Diaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Diaz_(Filipino_politician) "Antonio Diaz (Filipino politician)"), nephew; former Congressman and Assemblyman of Zambales
*   [Anita Magsaysay-Ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Magsaysay-Ho "Anita Magsaysay-Ho"), cousin; painter

### House of Representatives (1945–1950)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: House of Representatives (1945–1950)")]

On April 22, 1946, Magsaysay, encouraged by his fellow ex-guerrillas, was elected under the [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(Philippines) "Liberal Party (Philippines)") to the [Philippine House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_House_of_Representatives "Philippine House of Representatives").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Ramon_Magsaysay_2008-2) In 1948, President [Manuel Roxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Roxas "Manuel Roxas") chose Magsaysay to go to [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") as Chairman of the Committee on Guerrilla Affairs, to help secure the passage of the Rogers Veterans Bill, giving benefits to Philippine veterans.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In the so-called ["dirty election" of 1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Philippine_general_election "1949 Philippine general election"), he was re-elected to a second term in the House of Representatives. During both terms, he was Chairman of the House National Defense Committee.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Secretary of National Defense (1950–1953)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Secretary of National Defense (1950–1953)")]

[![Image 11: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(March 2011)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

In early August 1950, he offered President [Elpidio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino "Elpidio Quirino") a plan to fight the communist guerrillas, using his own experiences in guerrilla warfare during World War II. After some hesitation, Quirino realized that there was no alternative and appointed Magsaysay Secretary of National Defense in September 1950.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Thompson-2014-9) He intensified the campaign against the [Hukbalahap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hukbalahap "Hukbalahap") guerrillas. This success was due in part to the unconventional methods he took up from a former advertising expert and CIA agent, Colonel [Edward Lansdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Lansdale "Edward Lansdale"). In the counterinsurgency the two utilized deployed soldiers distributing relief goods and other forms of aid to outlying, provincial communities. Prior to Magsaysay's appointment as Defense Secretary, rural citizens perceived the Philippine Army with apathy and distrust. However, Magsaysay's term enhanced the Army's image, earning them respect and admiration.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-10)

In June 1952, Magsaysay made a goodwill tour to the United States and Mexico. He visited [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") (with a medical check-up at [Walter Reed Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Reed_Army_Medical_Center "Walter Reed Army Medical Center")) and [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City"), where he spoke at the Annual Convention of [Lions International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lions_International "Lions International").

By 1953, President Quirino thought the threat of the Huks was under control and Secretary Magsaysay was becoming too weak. Magsaysay met with interference and obstruction from the President and his advisers, in fears they might be unseated at the next presidential election. Although Magsaysay had at that time no intention to run, he was urged from many sides and finally was convinced that the only way to continue his fight against communism, and for a government for the people, was to be elected president, ousting the corrupt administration that, in his opinion, had caused the rise of the communist guerrillas by bad administration. He resigned his post as defense secretary on February 28, 1953,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Barrens-1970-11) and became the presidential candidate of the [Nacionalista Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista_Party_(Philippines) "Nacionalista Party (Philippines)"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Simbulan-2005-12) disputing the nomination with Senator [Camilo Osías](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camilo_Os%C3%ADas "Camilo Osías") at the Nacionalista national convention.

#### 1951 Padilla incident

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1951 Padilla incident")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/83/Moises_Padilla_Story.jpg/250px-Moises_Padilla_Story.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Moises_Padilla_Story.jpg)

Theatrical poster of the 1961 film _The Moises Padilla Story_ that narrates the 1951 event.

When news reached Magsaysay that his political ally Moises Padilla was being [tortured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture "Torture") by men of provincial governor Rafael Lacson, he rushed to [Negros Occidental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negros_Occidental "Negros Occidental"), but was too late. He was then informed that Padilla's body was drenched in blood, pierced by fourteen bullets, and was positioned on a police bench in the town plaza.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-time_1954-13) Magsaysay himself carried Padilla's corpse with his bare hands and delivered it to the [morgue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgue "Morgue"), and the next day, news clips showed pictures of him doing so.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Pimentel-14) Magsaysay even used this event during his [presidential campaign in 1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Philippine_general_election "1953 Philippine general election").

The trial against Lacson started in January 1952; Magsaysay and his men presented enough evidence to convict Lacson and his 26 men for murder.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-time_1954-13) In August 1954, Judge Eduardo Enríquez ruled the men were guilty and Lacson, his 25 men and three other mayors of Negros Occidental municipalities were condemned to the [electric chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_chair "Electric chair").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-15)

### Manila Railroad leadership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Manila Railroad leadership")]

Magsaysay was also the general manager of the [Manila Railroad Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Railroad_Company "Manila Railroad Company") between October and December 1951. His tenure later motivated him to modernize the rail operator's fleet after stepping into presidency. He also set the first steps in building what has been the discontinued Cagayan Valley Railroad Extension project.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-16)

### 1953 presidential campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 1953 presidential campaign")]

Main article: [1953 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Philippine_presidential_election "1953 Philippine presidential election")

Presidential elections were held on November 10, 1953, in the Philippines. Incumbent President [Elpidio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino "Elpidio Quirino") lost his opportunity for a second full term as [President of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines") to former Defense Secretary Magsaysay. His running mate, [Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Philippines "Senate of the Philippines")[José Yulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Yulo "José Yulo") lost to [Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Philippines "Senate of the Philippines")[Carlos P. García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_P._Garc%C3%ADa "Carlos P. García"). [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines "Vice President of the Philippines")[Fernando López](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Lopez "Fernando Lopez") did not run for re-election. This was the first time that an elected Philippine President did not come from the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Philippines "Senate of the Philippines"). Moreover, Magsaysay began the practice in the Philippines of "campaign jingles" during elections, for one of his inclinations and hobbies was dancing. The jingles that were used during the election period was ["Mambo Magsaysay"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qJyuARjSo0M&pp=ygUPbWFtYm8gbWFnc2F5c2F5)", ["We Want Magsaysay"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YTzfWMJWA9s&pp=ygURd2Ugd2FudCBtYWdzYXlzYXk%3D), and ["The Magsaysay Mambo"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DkEp0lXT32Q)

The [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government "United States government"), including the [Central Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency"), had strong influence on the 1953 election, and candidates in the election fiercely competed with each other for U.S. support.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Tharoor-18)

In the [election of 1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Philippine_general_election "1953 Philippine general election"), Magsaysay was decisively elected president over the incumbent [Elpidio Quirino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elpidio_Quirino "Elpidio Quirino"). He was sworn into office on Wednesday, December 30, 1953, at the [Independence Grandstand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_Grandstand "Quirino Grandstand") in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-19) He was wearing the [barong tagalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barong_tagalog "Barong tagalog"), a first by a Philippine President and a tradition that still continues up to this day. He was then called "[Mambo Magsaysay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambo_Magsaysay "Mambo Magsaysay")". Also dressed in [barong tagalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barong_tagalog "Barong tagalog") was the elected vice-president [Carlos P. Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_P._Garcia "Carlos P. Garcia").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Halili,_M.C._2010-20) The oath of office was administered by [Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines")[Ricardo Paras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Paras "Ricardo Paras"). For the first time, a Philippine president swore on the [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible "Bible") on an inauguration.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-21) He swore on two Bibles, from each parents' side.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-bmelefante-22)

As President, he was a close friend and supporter of the United States and a vocal spokesman against communism during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"). He led the foundation of the [Southeast Asia Treaty Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia_Treaty_Organization "Southeast Asia Treaty Organization"), also known as the Manila Pact of 1954, that aimed to defeat communist-Marxist movements in Southeast Asia, South Asia, and the Southwestern Pacific.

During his term, he made [Malacañang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace") literally a "house of the people," opening its gates to the public. One example of his integrity followed a demonstration flight aboard a new plane belonging to the [Philippine Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Air_Force "Philippine Air Force") (PAF): President Magsaysay asked what the operating costs per hour were for that type of aircraft, then wrote a personal check to the PAF, covering the cost of his flight. He restored the people's trust in the military and in the government.

#### Presidential Inauguration Day

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Presidential Inauguration Day")]

Ushering a new era in [Philippine government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_government "Philippine government"), President Magsaysay placed emphasis upon service to the people by bringing the government closer to the former.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Molina,_Antonio_1961-3)

This was symbolically seen when, on inauguration day, President Magsaysay ordered the gates of [Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace") be opened to the general public, who were allowed to freely visit all parts of the palace complex. Later, this was regulated to allow weekly visitation.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Molina,_Antonio_1961-3)

He created the Presidential Complaints and Action Committee.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Molina,_Antonio_1961-3) This body immediately proceeded to hear grievances and recommend remedial action. Headed by [Manuel Manahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Manahan "Manuel Manahan"), this committee would come to hear nearly 60,000 complaints in a year, of which more than 30,000 would be settled by direct action and a little more than 25,000 would be referred to government agencies for appropriate follow-up. This new entity proved to be a success, increasing approval rates.

#### Agrarian reform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Agrarian reform")]

See also: [Land reform in the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_the_Philippines "Land reform in the Philippines")

To amplify and stabilize the functions of the Economic Development Corps (EDCOR), President Magsaysay worked for the establishment of the National Resettlement and Rehabilitation Administration (NARRA). This body took over from the EDCOR and helped in giving sixty-five thousand acres to 3000 indigent families for settlement purposes. It allocated some 1,500 to 25,000 landless families, who subsequently became [farmers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmers "Farmers").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Molina,_Antonio_1961-3)

As further aid to the rural people, the president established the Agricultural Credit and Cooperative Financing Administration (ACCFA). The idea was for this entity to make available rural credits. Records show that it granted almost ten million dollars. This administrative body then devoted its attention to cooperative marketing.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Molina,_Antonio_1961-3)

Along this line of help to the rural areas, President Magsaysay initiated the [artesian wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artesian_well "Artesian well") campaign. A group-movement known as the Liberty Wells Association was formed and in record time managed to raise a considerable sum for the construction of as many artesian wells as possible. The socio-economic value of the had a profound effect, and the people were welcoming in their gratitude.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Molina,_Antonio_1961-3)

Vast irrigation projects, as well as enhancement of the Ambuklao Power plant and other similar ones, went a long way towards bringing to reality the rural improvement program advocated by Magsaysay.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Molina,_Antonio_1961-3)

Magsaysay enacted the following laws as part of his Agrarian Reform Program:

*   Republic Act No. 1160 of 1954 – Abolished the LASEDECO and established the National Resettlement and Rehabilitation Administration (NARRA) to resettle dissidents and landless farmers. It was particularly aimed at rebel returnees providing home lots and farmlands in Palawan and Mindanao.
*   Republic Act No. 1199 (Agricultural Tenancy Act of 1954) – governed the relationship between landowners and tenant farmers by organizing share-tenancy and leasehold system. The law provided the security of tenure of tenants. It also created the Court of Agrarian Relations.
*   Republic Act No. 1400 (Land Reform Act of 1955) – Created the Land Tenure Administration (LTA) which was responsible for the acquisition and distribution of large tenanted rice and corn lands over 200 hectares for individuals and 600 hectares for corporations.
*   Republic Act No. 821 (Creation of Agricultural Credit Cooperative Financing Administration) – Provided small farmers and share tenants loans with low interest rates of six to eight percent.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-23)

#### Hukbong Bayan Laban sa Hapon

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Hukbong Bayan Laban sa Hapon")]

In early 1954, [Benigno Aquino Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_Jr. "Benigno Aquino Jr.") was appointed by President Magsaysay to act as his personal emissary to [Luis Taruc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Taruc "Luis Taruc"), leader of the rebel group, [Hukbalahap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hukbalahap "Hukbalahap").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-24) Under Lt. Col. Laureño Maraña, the former head of Force X of the 16th PC Company, assumed command of the 7th BCT, which had become one of the most effective forces against the Huks. Force X employed psychological warfare through combat intelligence and infiltration that relied on secrecy in planning, training, and execution of attack. The lessons learned from Force X and Nenita were combined in the 7th BCT.

With the all out anti-dissidence campaigns against the Huks, they numbered less than 2,000 by 1954 and without the protection and support of local supporters, active Huk resistance no longer presented a serious threat to Philippine security. From February to mid-September 1954, the largest anti-Huk operation, "Operation Thunder-Lightning" was conducted that resulted in Taruc's surrender on May 17. Further cleanup operations of the remaining guerrillas lasted throughout 1955, cutting their number to less than 1,000 by year's end.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-26)

#### Southeast Asia Treaty Organization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Southeast Asia Treaty Organization")]

The administration of President Magsaysay was active in the fight against the expansion of communism in Asia. He made the Philippines a member of the Southeast Asia Treaty Organization ([SEATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEATO "SEATO")), which was established in Manila on September 8, 1954, during the "Manila Conference".[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-27) Members of SEATO were alarmed at the possible victory of [North Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vietnam "North Vietnam") over [South Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Vietnam "South Vietnam"), which could spread communist ideology to other countries in the region. The possibility that a communist state can influence or cause other countries to adopt the same system of government is called the [domino theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domino_theory "Domino theory").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-ReferenceA-28)

The active coordination of the Magsaysay administration with the Japanese government led to the Reparation Agreement. This was an agreement between the two countries, obligating the Japanese government to pay $550 million as reparation for war damages to the Philippines.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-ReferenceA-28)

The SEATO agreement have proved to be unpopular among the Philippines' Asian neighbors, considering its original members were the U.S., [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), the [U.K.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.K. "U.K."), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan") and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), with the U.S. as its driving force. His support for South Vietnamese president [Ngo Dinh Diem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngo_Dinh_Diem "Ngo Dinh Diem") became unpopular to the Vietnamese public especially those in the north. Magsaysay also pressured Cambodian Prince [Norodom Sihanouk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norodom_Sihanouk "Norodom Sihanouk") for [Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodia "Cambodia") to join SEATO and claimed that the prince was violating Cambodia's non-alignment policy.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Dagdag-29):91–94

#### Defense Council

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramon_Magsaysay&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Defense Council")]

Taking the advantage of the presence of U.S. Secretary [John Foster Dulles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Foster_Dulles "John Foster Dulles") in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila") to attend the [SEATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEATO "SEATO") Conference, the Philippine government took steps to broach with him the establishment of a Joint Defense Council. Vice-President and Secretary of Foreign Affairs [Carlos P. Garcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_P._Garcia "Carlos P. Garcia") held the opportune conversations with Secretary Dulles for this purpose. Agreement was reached thereon and the first meeting of the Joint United States–Philippines Defense Council was held in Manila following the end of the Manila Conference. Thus were the terms of the Mutual Defense Pact between the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") and the United States duly implemented.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Magsaysay#cite_note-Molina,_Antonio_1961-3)
