**6. Samora Machel (1933-1986):** The president of Mozambique died in a plane crash near the Mozambican-South African border. The cause of the crash is disputed with some alleging South African involvement.

**7. Bingu wa Mutharika (1934-2012):** The president of Malawi died of a heart attack following a cardiac arrest on his way to a hospital in Lilongwe, Malawi after his presidential convoy was diverted due to his helicopter encountering bad weather.

**8. Hafez al-Assad (1930-2000):** The president of Syria died in a plane crash near Damascus. The crash occurred under mysterious circumstances with some suggesting foul play, although the official cause was attributed to a heart attack suffered by Assad while piloting the aircraft.

**10. Dag Hammarskjold (1905-1961):** The then Secretary-General of the United Nations died in a plane crash in Northern Rhodesia (now Zambia) in 1961.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Hungarian photographer (1912–1968)

The native form of this [personal name](link_2) is _Marton Ervin_.This article uses [Western name order](link_2) when mentioning individuals.

| Ervin Marton |
| --- |
| [![Image 4](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/ErvinMartonWikiCirca1940.png/250px-ErvinMartonWikiCirca1940.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ErvinMartonWikiCirca1940.png) Ervin Marton self-portrait, dancing – circa 1940 (detail) |
| Born | (1912-06-17)17 June 1912 [Budapest](link_3), Hungary |
| Died | 30 April 1968(1968-04-30) (aged 55) Paris, France |
| Occupations | * Photographer * Artist |
| Spouse | Martha Marton |
| Children | * Pier Marton * Yves Marton |

**Ervin Marton** (known as **Marton Ervin** in Hungarian; 17 June 1912 – 30 April 1968) was a Franco-Hungarian artist and photographer who became an integral part of the Paris art culture beginning in 1937. An internationally recognized photographer, he is known for his portraits of many key figures in art, literature and the sciences working in Paris, as well as for his candid "[street photography](link_4)". His work was regularly exhibited in Paris during his lifetime, as well as in Budapest, London and Milan. It is held by the [Hungarian National Gallery](link_5), the _[Bibliothèque Nationale](link_6)_ in Paris, and the Hungarian Museum of Photography, as well as by major corporations and private collectors in Europe and the United States.

Together with numerous other Hungarians and immigrants, Marton joined the [French Resistance](link_7) during the [Nazi](link_8)[occupation](link_9) of Paris in [World War II](link_10). Artists and intellectuals participated in projects of aiding refugees, printing clandestine communications to keep up morale, and forging passes to aid people trying to escape the Nazis. Afterwards, Marton was awarded the _[Médaille de la Libération](link_11)_ (French Liberation Medal) by the French government.

Renewed interest in the Hungarian artists of 20th-century Paris has generated major 21st-century exhibits of Ervin Marton and his contemporaries. These include exhibits in [Vienna](link_12), Austria (2004); and [Kecskemét](link_13) (2004) and [Budapest](link_3), Hungary (2007 and 2010). Marton's street photography of Paris was exhibited in California (2009) together with that of the 20th-century photographers [Inge Morath](link_14) and Max Yavno.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 2010–2011, Marton's photos of female nudes were exhibited with those of other Hungarian artists at the _Institut hongrois_ in Paris.

## Early life and education

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ervin_Marton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Ervin Marton was born in [Budapest](link_3), [Austria-Hungary](link_15), in 1912 to István Preisz and his wife Janka Csillag, a Hungarian-Jewish couple. He had two sisters. Marton started drawing as a child; and as a teenager, he began to work in photography, although he never studied it formally.

A cousin-in-law by marriage was [Lajos Tihanyi](link_16) (1885–1938), one of the Hungarian artists' circle known as [The Eight](link_17) (_Nyolcak_) (1909–1918 in Budapest), who became a renowned painter and [lithographer](link_18). In 1919, after the fall of the short-lived [Hungarian Soviet Republic](link_19), Tihanyi emigrated to [Vienna](link_12). He went on to [Berlin](link_20), where he became friends with [Brassaï](link_21) and other younger Hungarian artists and writers.[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-Brassai-1) After the Hungarian and Russian revolutions, many artists and intellectuals migrated to Berlin from Eastern and Central Europe. In the early 1920s, there was a "short-lived" synthesis here of the international avant-garde with artists and intellectuals of Western Europe.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-passuth2-2)

Lastly, Tihanyi emigrated to Paris in 1924, along with many other Hungarian artists,[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-Tihanyi-3), including Brassai and [André Kertész](link_22). After Ervin Marton went to Paris in 1937, Tihanyi introduced him to many of the friends in his large émigré circle.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-Cohen-4)

After completing his [Baccalaureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor [link_23]'s_degree "Bachelor's degree"), Marton continued his studies at the Omike Drawing School in Budapest, under the artist Manó Vestróczy.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-Kieselbach-5) He also studied at the Budapest Arts and Crafts Institute (1934–1937). During the summers from 1935 to 1937, he regularly spent time in [Kalocsa](link_24), about 90 miles south of Budapest. Marton was fascinated by the [Roma](link_25), whom he drew, painted and photographed there.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-Photo-6)

## Career

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ervin_Marton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

In the 1930s, Marton had his first exhibit at galleries in Budapest, when he was in his early 20s. His graphic art exhibit in 1936 at the Műterem (Studio) Gallery with Aladár Farkas[[note 1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-7) was praised by the critic Artur Elek of the _[Nyugat](link_26)_,[[note 2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-8) and the writers Mária Dutka and Ödön Gerő. Edit Hoffman purchased several of Marton's works from the exhibit for what became the Hungarian National Gallery (_Magyar Nemzeti Galéria_). Until 1946 and his father's death, Marton frequently signed his work using his father's name Preisz as a surname (Ervin Preisz), or sometimes using Paal (Paul).[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-Marton-9)

Marton became intrigued by the growing [Esperanto](link_27) movement and its concept that using one language would bring people together. He accepted a commission for a series of stamps that celebrated Esperantist ideals.

### War years in Paris

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ervin_Marton&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: War years in Paris")]

In 1937, Marton moved to Paris, a centre for artists and writers from across Europe and a refuge for Jews suffering [anti-Semitism](link_28) in their native lands of Germany and eastern Europe. He became part of the vibrant circle of Hungarian émigré artists. Marton continued to study as well. He took classes in painting and sculpture at the [École des Beaux-Arts](link_29).

Through his cousin, the painter [Lajos Tihanyi](link_16) (who died in 1938), Marton became part of an older circle of established artists and writers. He got to know the photographer Brassai and the writer György Bölöni.[[note 3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-10)[[note 4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-11) Marton also became connected to the writer Andor Németh and the painter [Bertalan Pór](link_30). The latter was one of [The Eight](link_31) with Tihanyi in Budapest before World War I, and both men were also friends of Brassaï.[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ervin_Marton#cite_note-Brassai-1) Although Kertész had emigrated to New York City in 1936, he and Marton became friends during his regular trips to Europe.
